script:
GTA 6 is predicted to make over $1 billion in its first week, yet the actress playing Lucia almost certainly isn't a millionaire from it. Why doesn't a massive payday for a game company flow down to its star?

In video games, voice and motion-capture actors usually sign buyout contracts. Instead of taking a slice of the game's profits, they get paid a flat union day rate—often around $1,000 per 4-hour session.

Even if an actor works 100 sessions over 3 years of production, that stack of checks adds up to roughly $100,000 before taxes and agent fees. Meanwhile, the publisher keeps 100% of the billion-dollar sales chart.

Compare that to a movie star who negotiates backend points, where a tiny 2% cut of box office tickets sends millions straight into their bank account. Video game contracts rarely share the upside like that.

A big title doesn't always mean big wealth—the real money goes to whoever owns the asset, not the person trading hours for a paycheck. Subscribe to PocketIQ for more smart money truths!
